An Analytic Propositional Proof System on Graphs
Matteo Acclavio, Ross Horne, Lutz Straßburger

Abstract
. In this paper we present a proof system that operates on graphs instead of formulas. Starting from the well-known relationship between formulas and cographs, we drop the cograph-conditions and look at arbitrary (undirected) graphs. This means that we lose the tree structure of the formulas corresponding to the cographs, and we can no longer use standard proof theoretical methods that depend on that tree structure. In order to overcome this difficulty, we use a modular decomposition of graphs and some techniques from deep inference where inference rules do not rely on the main connective of a formula. For our proof system we show the admissibility of cut and a generalisation of the splitting property. Finally, we show that our system is a conservative extension of multiplicative linear logic with mix, and we argue that our graphs form a notion of generalised connective.

Introduction

The notion of formula is central to all applications of logic and
proof theory in computer science, ranging from the formal verification
of software, where a formula describes a property that the program
should satisfy, to logic programming, where a formula represents a
program
[
MNPS91
,
KY93
]
, and functional programming, where a
formula represents a type
[
How80
]
. Proof theoretical methods
are also employed in concurrency theory, where a formula can represent a
process whose behaviours may be extracted from a proof of the formula
[
Mil93
,
Bru02
,
FRS01
,
DSC16
,
OP17
,
NOP17
,
HT19
,
Hor19
,
Hor20
]
.
This
formulas-as-processes
paradigm
is not as well-investigated as the
formulas-as-properties
,

formulas-as-programs
and
formulas-as-types
paradigms
mentioned before. In our opinion, a reason for this is that
the notion of formula reaches its limitations when it comes to
describing processes as they are studied in concurrency theory.

For example, Guglielmi’s
BV

[
Gug07
]
and Retoré’s
pomset
logic

[
Ret97
]

are proof systems which extend linear logic with a notion of
sequential composition and can model series-parallel orders.
1
1

1

In his PhD-thesis
[
Ret93
]
, Retoré considers all partial ordered multisets, but in later versions
[
Ret21
]
only series-parallel orders are considered to maintain the correspondence to formulas.
,
2
2

2

It has long been believed that
BV
and pomset
logic are the same, but recently it has been shown that this is not the case
[
NS22a
,
NS22b
]
.

However,
series-parallel orders cannot express some ubiquitous patterns of

causal dependencies
such as the logical time constraints on producer-consumer
queues
[
LW00
]
, which are within the scope of
pomsets
[
Pra86
]
, event structures
[
NPW81
]
, and
Petri nets
[
Pet77
]
. The essence of this problem is already
visible when we consider
symmetric dependencies
, such as
separation, which happens to be the dual
concept to concurrency in the
formulas-as-processes

paradigm.

Let us use some simple examples to explain the problem. Suppose we are
in a situation where two processes
A
and
B
can communicate with
each other, written as
A\mathbin{\invamp}B
, or are separated from each
other, written as
A\mathbin{\otimes}B
, such that no communication is
possible. Now assume we have four atomic processes
a
,
b
,
c
, and

d
, from which we form the two processes
P=(a\mathbin{\otimes}b)\mathbin{\invamp}(c\mathbin{\otimes}d)
and
Q=(a\mathbin{\invamp}c)\mathbin{\otimes}(b\mathbin{\invamp}d)
. Both are perfectly fine
formulas of multiplicative linear logic (
\mathsf{MLL}
)
[
Gir87a
]
.
In

P
, we have that
a
is separated from
b
but can communicate with

c
and
d
. Similarly,
d
can communicate with
a
and
b
but is
separated from
c
, and so on. On the other hand, in
Q
,
a
can only
communicate with
c
and is separated from the other two, and
d

can only communicate with
b
, and is separated from the other
two. We can visualise this situation via graphs where
a
,
b
,
c
,
and
d
are the vertices, and we draw an edge between two vertices if
they are separated, and no edge if they can communicate. Then
P

and
Q
correspond to the two graphs shown below.

\begin{array}[]{c@{\qquad}c}P=(a\mathbin{\otimes}b)\mathbin{\invamp}(c\mathbin{\otimes}d)&Q=(a\mathbin{\invamp}c)\mathbin{\otimes}(b\mathbin{\invamp}d)\\[4.30554pt]

(2)

An example of this behaviour could arise in the setting of concurrent processes, where four processes
a
,
b
,
c
, and
d

satisfy information flow constraints such that

c
and
a
can communicate;

a
and
d
can communicate; and

d
and
b
can communicate,
and no further communications are possible.
This models an intransitive information flow,
since we have two processes,
a
and
d
, which can communicate with each other, and respectively with
c
and
b
;
yet the same processes must also ensure that no information flows between
c
and
b
.
However, the graph (
2
) cannot be described by a formula in the way illustrated for
the two graphs in (
1
).

This means that the tools of
proof theory, which have been developed over the course of the last
century and which were very successful for the

formulas-as-properties
,
formulas-as-programs
, and

formulas-as-types
paradigms, cannot be used for the

formulas-as-processes
paradigm unless we forbid situations as
in (
2
) above. This seems to be a very strong
and unnatural restriction (that is, it is an
a posteri
restriction imposed by the use of formulas, with no
a priory
justification stemming from process modelling problems). The purpose of this paper is to propose
a way to change this unsatisfactory situation.

We will present a proof system, called
\mathsf{GS}
(for
graphical
proof system
), whose objects of reason are not formulas but graphs,
giving the example in (
2
) the same status as the examples in (
1
).
In a less informal way, one could say that standard
proof systems work on cographs (which are the class of graphs that
correspond to formulas as in (
1
)
[
Duf65
]
), and our proof systems works
on arbitrary graphs. In order for this to make sense, our proof
system should obey the following basic properties:

(1)

Consistency
: There are graphs that are not provable.
In particular, if only a finite number of graphs is provable (or not provable) then the proof system would not be interesting.

(2)

Transitivity
: The proof
system should come with an implication that is transitive, i.e., if
we can prove that
A
implies
B
and that
B
implies
C
, then we
should also be able to prove that
A
implies
C
.

(3)

Analyticity
: As we no longer have formulas, we cannot ask
that every formula that occurs in a proof is a subformula of its
conclusion. However, we can investigate a graph theoretical version of this idea, and we can ask that in a proof search situation, there
is always only a finite number of ways
to apply an
inference rule.

(4)

Minimality
: We want to make as few assumptions as
possible,
so that the theory we develop is as general as possible.

Properties
1
-
3
are standard for any proof system, and they are usually
proved using cut elimination. In that respect our paper is no
different. We introduce a notion of cut and show its
admissibility for
\mathsf{GS}
. Then Properties 1-3 are immediate consequences.

Property
4
is of a more subjective nature. In our case, we only make
the following two basic assumptions:

(1)

For any graph
A
, we should be able to prove that
A

implies
A
.
This assumption is almost impossible to argue against, so can be expected for any logic.

(2)

If a graph
A
is provable, then the graph
G=C[A]

is also provable, provided that

C[\cdot]
is a provable context.
3
3

3

Formally, the notation
G=C[A]
means that

A
is a module of
G
, and
C[\cdot]
is the graph obtained
from
G
by removing all vertices belonging to
A
. We give the
formal definition in Section
3
.
This can be compared to the

necessitation rule
of modal logic, which says that if
A
is
provable then so is
\Box A
, except that in our case the
\Box

is replaced by the provable graph context
C[\cdot]
.

All other properties of the system
\mathsf{GS}
follow from the need to
obtain admissibility of cut. This means that this paper does not
present some random system, but follows the underlying principles of
proof theory.
For a more detailed philosophical presentation of these principles, we refer the reader to Appendix
B
.

We also target the desirable property of
conservativity
.
This means that there should be a well-known logic
\mathsf{L}

(based on formulas) such that the restriction of our proof system to
those graphs that correspond to formulas proves exactly the
theorems of
\mathsf{L}
.
This cannot be an assumption used to design a logical system, since it would create circularity (to specify a logic we need a logic); conservativity is more so a cultural sanity condition to check that we have not invented an esoteric logic.
In our case, conservativity will follow from cut admissibility, and
the logic
\mathsf{L}
is multiplicative linear logic with mix (
\mathsf{MLL^{\circ}}
)
[
Gir87a
,
Bel97
,
FR94
]
.

Let us now summarise how this paper is organised:
In
Section
2
, we give preliminaries on cographs, which
form the class of graphs that correspond to formulas as
in (
1
). Then, in Section
3
we give some
preliminaries on modules and prime graphs, which are needed for our
move away from cographs, so that in Section
4
, we can
present our proof system, which uses the notation of open
deduction
[
GGP10
]
and follows the principles of deep
inference
[
GS01
,
BT01
,
Gug07
]
. To our
knowledge, this is the first proof system that is not tied to
formulas/cographs but handles arbitrary (undirected) graphs instead.
In Section
5
we show some properties of our system,
and
Sections
6
and
7

are dedicated to cut elimination, which is the basis for showing properties (
1
), (
2
), and (
3
), mentioned above.
We also explain the technology we must develop in order to be able
to prove cut elimination for our proof system.
The interesting point
is that, not only do we go beyond methods developed for the sequent
calculus, but we also go beyond methods developed for deep inference
on formulas. In particular, we require entirely new statements of the
tools called
splitting
and
context reduction
, and
furthermore their proofs are inter-dependent, whereas normally context
reduction follows from splitting
[
GS11
,
ATG18
]
.

Then, in
Section
8
, we not only show that our system is a conservative
extension of
\mathsf{MLL^{\circ}}
, we also show a form of analyticity for our system.
Finally, in Section
9
, we
show how our work is related to the work on generalised
connectives
introduced in
[
Gir87b
,
DR89
]
.
We end this paper with a discussion of related work in
Section
10

and a
conclusion in Section
11
.

Compared to the conference version
[
AHS20
]
of this paper, there are the following three major additions:

•

We give detailed proofs of the
Splitting Lemma
and the

Context Reduction Lemma
(in Section
6
and Appendix
A
),
which are crucial for the cut elimination proof. In fact, we also
completely reorganised the proofs with respect to the technical
appendix of
[
AHS20
]
4
4

4

That appendix is available
at
https://hal.inria.fr/hal-02560105
.
. For proving these
lemmas, we could not rely on the general method that has been
proposed by Aler Tubella in her PhD
[
AT17
]
.

•

We present a notion of analyticity for proof systems on graphs and
show that our system is analytic in that respect (in
Section
8
).

•

We show that general graphs with
n
vertices can be seen as
generalised
n
-ary connectives (in Section
9
),
and we compare this notion with the existing notion of generalised
(multiplicative)
connective
[
Gir87b
,
DR89
,
Mai19
,
AM20
]
.

•

We include in Appendix
B
a more detailed discussion of
how our proof system can be considered satisfactory with respect to
the Properties (
1
)–(
4
) mentioned above.

Finally, let us argue that logics are not designed but discovered. They typically follow logical principles where design parameters are limited.

(3)

There is no pre-existing semantics or proof system we can refer to at this point.
Nonetheless, from the above discussed principles we can argue, that in a logic on graphs, the former implication in (
3
) cannot hold while the latter must hold.
Over the course of this paper, we explore the design of proof systems on graphs based on logical principles, which enables us to confidently state such facts.

2.
From Formulas to Graphs

In this preliminary section we recall the basic textbook definitions for graphs and formulas, and their correspondence via cographs.

{defi}

A
(simple, undirected) graph

G
is a pair

\langle V_{G},E_{G}\rangle
where
V_{G}
is a set of vertices and
E_{G}
is a
set of two-element subsets of
V_{G}
. We omit the index
G
when it
is clear from the context. For
v,w\in V_{G}
we write
vw
as an abbreviation
for
\{v,w\}
. A graph
G
is
finite
if its vertex set

V_{G}
is finite. Let
L
be a set and
G
be a graph. We say that

G
is
L
-labelled
(or just
labelled
if

L
is clear from the context) if every vertex in
V_{G}
is associated
with an element of
L
, called its
label
. We write

\ell_{G}(v)
to denote the label of the vertex
v
in
G
. A
graph
G^{\prime}
is a
subgraph
of a graph
G
, denoted as

G^{\prime}\subseteq G
iff
V_{G^{\prime}}\subseteq V_{G}
and
E_{G^{\prime}}\subseteq E_{G}
. We
say that
G^{\prime}
is an
induced subgraph
of
G
if
G^{\prime}
is
a subgraph of
G
and for all
v,w\in V_{G^{\prime}}
, if
vw\in E_{G}
then

vw\in E_{G^{\prime}}
. For a graph
G
we write
|V_{G}|
for its number of vertices and
|E_{G}|
for its number of edges.

In the following, we will just say
graph
to mean a finite,
undirected, labelled graph, where the labels come from the set
\mathcal{A}

of atoms which is the (disjoint) union of a countable set of
propositional variables
\mathcal{V}=\{a,b,c,\ldots\}
and their duals

{\mathcal{V}^{\bot}}=\{{a^{\bot}},{b^{\bot}},{c^{\bot}},\ldots\}
.

Since we are mainly interested in how vertices are labelled, but not so much in the identity of the underlying vertex,
we heavily rely on the notion of graph isomorphism.

{defi}

Two graphs
G
and
G^{\prime}
are
isomorphic
if there exists a
bijection
f\colon V_{G}\rightarrow V_{G^{\prime}}
such that for all

v,u\in V_{G}
we have
vu\in E_{G}
iff
f(v)f(u)\in E_{G^{\prime}}
and

\ell_{G}(v)=\ell_{G^{\prime}}(f(v))
. We denote this as

G\simeq_{f}G^{\prime}
, or simply as
G\simeq G^{\prime}
if
f
is clear from the context
or not relevant.

In the following, we will, in diagrams, forget the identity of the
underlying vertices, showing only the label, as in the examples in the
introduction.

In the rest of this section we recall the characterisation of those
graphs that correspond to formulas. For simplicity, we restrict
ourselves to only two connectives, and for reasons that will become
clear later, we use the
\mathbin{\invamp}
(
par
) and
\mathbin{\otimes}

(
tensor
) of linear logic
[
Gir87a
]
. More precisely,

formulas
are generated by the grammar

\phi,\psi\Coloneqq\mathord{\circ}\mid a\mid{a^{\bot}}\mid\phi\mathbin{\invamp}\psi\mid\phi\mathbin{\otimes}\psi

(4)

where
\mathord{\circ}
is the
unit
, and
a
can stand for any
propositional variable in
\mathcal{V}
. As usual, we can define the negation
of formulas inductively by letting

{a^{\bot\bot}}=a
for all
a\in\mathcal{V}
, and by
using the De Morgan duality between
\mathbin{\invamp}

and
\mathbin{\otimes}
:
{(\phi\mathbin{\invamp}\psi)^{\bot}}={\phi^{\bot}}\mathbin{\otimes}{\psi^{\bot}}
and

{(\phi\mathbin{\otimes}\psi)^{\bot}}={\phi^{\bot}}\mathbin{\invamp}{\psi^{\bot}}
; the unit is
self-dual:
{\mathord{\circ}^{\bot}}=\mathord{\circ}
.

On formulas we
define the following structural equivalence relation:

\begin{array}[]{r@{~}l@{\hskip 4em}r@{~}l}\phi\mathbin{\invamp}(\psi\mathbin{\invamp}\xi)\equiv&(\phi\mathbin{\invamp}\psi)\mathbin{\invamp}\xi\hfil\hskip 40.00006pt&\phi\mathbin{\otimes}(\psi\mathbin{\otimes}\xi)\equiv&(\phi\mathbin{\otimes}\psi)\mathbin{\otimes}\xi\\
\phi\mathbin{\invamp}\psi\equiv&\psi\mathbin{\invamp}\phi\hfil\hskip 40.00006pt&\phi\mathbin{\otimes}\psi\equiv&\psi\mathbin{\otimes}\phi\\
\phi\mathbin{\invamp}\mathord{\circ}\equiv&\phi\hfil\hskip 40.00006pt&\phi\mathbin{\otimes}\mathord{\circ}\equiv&\phi\end{array}

(5)

In order to translate formulas to graphs, we define the following two
operations on graphs:

{defi}

Let
G=\langle V_{G},E_{G}\rangle
and
H=\langle V_{H},E_{H}\rangle
be graphs. We define the
par
of
G
and
H
to be their disjoint union and the
tensor
to be their join, i.e.:

\displaystyle G\mathbin{\invamp}H

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\langle V_{G}\uplus V_{H},E_{G}\uplus E_{H}\rangle

\displaystyle G\mathbin{\otimes}H

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\langle V_{G}\uplus V_{H},E_{G}\uplus E_{H}\uplus\{vw\mid v\in V_{G},w\in V_{H}\}\rangle

These operations can be visualised as follows:

\begin{array}[]{c@{\qquad\qquad\qquad\;}c}G\mathbin{\invamp}H&G\mathbin{\otimes}H\\

(6)

For a formula
\phi
, we can now define its associated
graph
\llbracket\phi\rrbracket
inductively as follows:

\llbracket\mathord{\circ}\rrbracket=\varnothing
the empty graph;
\llbracket a\rrbracket=a
a single-vertex graph whose vertex is labelled by
a
(by a slight abuse
of notation, we denote that graph also by
a
); similarly

\llbracket{a^{\bot}}\rrbracket={a^{\bot}}
; finally we define

\llbracket\phi\mathbin{\invamp}\psi\rrbracket=\llbracket\phi\rrbracket\mathbin{\invamp}\llbracket\psi\rrbracket
and

\llbracket\phi\mathbin{\otimes}\psi\rrbracket=\llbracket\phi\rrbracket\mathbin{\otimes}\llbracket\psi\rrbracket
.

Theorem 1
.

For any two formulas,
\phi\equiv\psi
iff
\llbracket\phi\rrbracket\simeq\llbracket\psi\rrbracket
.

Proof 2.1
.

By a straightforward induction.

(7)

The following result is classical and its proof can be found, e.g., in
[
Möh89
]
or
[
Gug07
]
.

Theorem 3

(
[
Duf65
]
)
.

Let
G
be a graph. Then there is a formula
\phi
with
\llbracket\phi\rrbracket\simeq G
iff
G
is
\mathsf{P_{4}}
-free.

The graphs characterised by Theorem
3

are called

Definition 4
.

cographs, because they are the smallest class of
graphs containing all single-vertex graphs and being closed under
complement and disjoint union.

Because of Theorem
3
, one can think of standard proof
systems as
cograph proof systems
.
Since in this paper we want to move from cographs to general graphs,
we need to investigate how much of the tree structure of formulas
(which makes cographs so interesting for proof theory
[
Ret03
,
Hug06
,
Str17
]
)
can be recovered for general graphs.

3.
Modules and Prime Graphs

One of the consequences of the tree structure of formulas is the notion of
subformula
, which is induced by the notion of subtree. This is lost if we move from cographs to general graphs. However, in a cograph
G
, a
module
of
G
corresponds to a subformula of the formula
\phi
given by Theorem
3
. The notion of module also exists for general graphs, and in our proof systems on graphs, modules will play a similar role as subformulas play in ordinary proof systems on formulas.

For this reason, we recall here some standard results on graph modules and the modular decomposition of graphs
[
MR84
,
EHR99
,
CD08
,
HP10
]
.

{defi}

Let
G
be a graph. A

Definition 5
.

module of
G
is an induced
subgraph
M=\langle V_{M},E_{M}\rangle
of
G
such that for all

v\in V_{G}\setminus V_{M}
and all
x,y\in V_{M}
we have
vx\in E_{G}
iff

vy\in E_{G}
.

{nota}

Let
M
be a module of a graph
G
,
and
let
C
be the graph obtained from
G

by removing all vertices in
M
(including incident edges).
If

R\subseteq V_{C}
is the set of vertices that are in
G
connected to a
vertex in
V_{M}
(and hence to all vertices in
M
by modularity),
then we write
G=C[M]_{R}

and we say that
C[\cdot]_{R}
is the

Definition 6
.

context of
M
in
G
.

Alternatively, we can consider a context

C[\cdot]_{R}
as a graph with a distinguished vertex
[\cdot]

such that

R
is the set of neighbours of
[\cdot]
.
In this case
C[M]_{R}
can be defined as
the graph obtained from
C[\cdot]R
by substituting the vertex
[\cdot]

with the graph
M
and adding
all the edges from each vertex in
V_{M}
to each vertex in
R
.

Finally, if we replace the hole with the empty graph we obtain the graph on the right above.

Lemma 3.1
.

Let
G
be a graph and
M,N
be modules of
G
. Then

(1)

M\cap N
is a module of
G
;

(2)

if
M\cap N\neq\varnothing
, then
M\cup N
is a module of
G
; and

(3)

if
N\not\subseteq M
then
M\setminus N
is a module of
G
.

Proof 3.2
.

The first statement follows immediately from the definition. For the
second one, let
L=M\cap N\neq\varnothing
, and let

v\in G\setminus(V_{M}\cup V_{N})
and
x,y\in V_{M}\cup V_{N}
. If
x,y
are
both in
M
or both in
N
, then we have immediately
vx\in E_{G}

iff
vy\in E_{G}
. So, let
x\in V_{M}
and
y\in V_{N}
, and let

z\in L
. We have
vx\in E_{G}
iff
vz\in E_{G}
iff

vy\in E_{G}
. Finally, for the last statement, let

x,y\in V_{M}\setminus V_{N}
and let

v\in V_{G}\setminus(V_{M}\setminus V_{N})
. If
v\notin V_{M}
, we immediately
have
vx\in E_{G}
iff
vy\in E_{G}
. So, let
v\in V_{M}
, and therefore

v\in V_{M}\cap V_{N}
. Let
z\in V_{N}\setminus V_{M}
. Then
vx\in E_{G}
iff

zx\in E_{G}
iff
zy\in E_{G}
iff
vy\in E_{G}
.

{defi}

Let
G
be a graph. A module
M
in
G
is

Definition 7
.

maximal if

M\neq G
and
for all modules
M^{\prime}\neq G
of
G

we have that

M\subseteq M^{\prime}
implies
M=M^{\prime}
.

{defi}

A module
M
of a graph
G
is

Definition 8
.

trivial iff either

V_{M}=\varnothing
or
V_{M}
is a singleton or
V_{M}=V_{G}
. A graph
G

is

Definition 9
.

prime iff
|V_{G}|\geq 2
and all modules of
G
are trivial.

{defi}

Let
G
be a graph with
n
vertices
V_{G}=\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{n}\}

and let
H_{1},\ldots,H_{n}
be
n
graphs. We define the

Definition 10
.

composition of
H_{1},\ldots,H_{n}
via
G
, denoted as

G\llparenthesis H_{1},\ldots,H_{n}\rrparenthesis
, by replacing each vertex
v_{i}
of
G

by the graph
H_{i}
; and there is an edge between two vertices
x

and
y
if either
x
and
y
are in the same
H_{i}
and

xy\in E_{H_{i}}
or
x\in V_{H_{i}}
and
y\in V_{H_{j}}
for
i\neq j
and

v_{i}v_{j}\in E_{G}
. Formally,

G\llparenthesis H_{1},\ldots,H_{n}\rrparenthesis=\langle V^{\ast},E^{\ast}\rangle
with

V^{\ast}=\biguplus_{1\leq i\leq n}V_{H_{i}}\quad\quad\mbox{and}\quad\quad E^{\ast}=\left(\biguplus_{1\leq i\leq n}E_{H_{i}}\right)\uplus\left\{xy\mid x\in V_{H_{i}},y\in V_{H_{j}},v_{i}v_{j}\in E_{G}\right\}

This concept allows us to decompose graphs into prime graphs (via
Lemma
3.3
below) and recover a tree structure for an
arbitrary graph.
5
5

5

This also allows us to consider prime graphs as generalised non-decomposable

n
-ary connectives. We will come back to this point in Section
9
.

(9)

We have
\mathbin{\invamp}\llparenthesis G,H\rrparenthesis=G\mathbin{\invamp}H
and
\mathbin{\otimes}\llparenthesis G,H\rrparenthesis=G\mathbin{\otimes}H
.

Lemma 3.3

(
[
Gal67
]
)
.

For every non-empty graph
G
we have exactly one of the following four cases:

(1)

G
is a singleton graph.

(2)

G=A\mathbin{\invamp}B
for some
A
,
B
with
A\neq\varnothing\neq B
.

(3)

G=A\mathbin{\otimes}B
for some
A
,
B
with
A\neq\varnothing\neq B
.

(4)

G=P\llparenthesis A_{1},\ldots,A_{n}\rrparenthesis
for some prime graph
P

with
n=|V_{P}|\geq 4
and
A_{i}\neq\varnothing
for every
i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}
.

Proof 3.4
.

Let
G
be given. If
|G|=1
, we are in case (i). Now
assume
|G|>1
, and let
M_{1},\ldots,M_{n}
be the maximal
modules of
G
. Note that
n\geq 2
. Now we have two cases:

•

For all
i,j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}
with
i\neq j
we have

M_{i}\cap M_{j}=\varnothing
. Since every vertex of
G
forms a
module, every vertex must be part of a maximal module. Hence

V_{G}=V_{M_{1}}\cup\cdots\cup V_{M_{n}}
. Therefore
there is a graph
P
such that

G=P\llparenthesis M_{1},\ldots,M_{n}\rrparenthesis
. Since all
M_{i}
are maximal in

G
, we can conclude that
P
is prime. If
|V_{P}|\geq 4

we are in case (iv). If
|V_{P}|<4
we are either in case
(ii) or (iii), as the two graphs in (
9
) are only
two prime graphs with
|V_{P}|=2
, and there are no prime
graphs with
|V_{P}|=3
.

•

We have some
i\neq j
with
M_{i}\cap M_{j}\neq\varnothing
. Let

L=M_{i}\cap M_{j}
and
N=M_{i}\setminus M_{j}
and

K=M_{j}\setminus M_{i}
. By Lemma
3.1
,
L
,
N
,

K
, and
M_{i}\cup M_{j}
are all modules of
G
. Since
M_{i}

and
M_{j}
are maximal, it follows that
G=M_{i}\cup M_{j}
, and
therefore
G=N\mathbin{\otimes}L\mathbin{\otimes}K
or
G=N\mathbin{\invamp}L\mathbin{\invamp}K
.

(11)

The modular decomposition tree can also be written in “formula style” as

\mathsf{P}_{4}\llparenthesis f\mathbin{\invamp}g,\mathsf{P}_{4}\llparenthesis a,b,c,d\rrparenthesis,{f^{\bot}}\mathbin{\otimes}{g^{\bot}},\mathsf{P}_{4}\llparenthesis{a^{\bot}},{b^{\bot}},{c^{\bot}},{d^{\bot}}\rrparenthesis\rrparenthesis

(12)

In the rest of the paper we will use all four representations
in (
10
) and (
11
) and (
12
)
interchangeably.

4.
The Proof System

To define a proof system on graphs, we need a notion of implication on graphs. To do
so, we first introduce a notion of negation on graphs.

{defi}

For a graph
G=\langle V_{G},E_{G}\rangle
, we define its

Definition 11
.

dual

{G^{\bot}}=\langle V_{G},E_{{G^{\bot}}}\rangle
to have the same set of vertices, and an
edge
vw\in E_{{G^{\bot}}}
iff
vw\notin E_{G}
(and
v\neq w
). The label of a vertex
v
in

{G^{\bot}}
is the dual of the label of that vertex in
G
, i.e.,

\ell_{{G^{\bot}}}(v)={\ell_{G}(v)^{\bot}}
. For any two graphs
G
and
H
, the

Definition 12
.

implication
G\multimap H
is defined to be the graph

{G^{\bot}}\mathbin{\invamp}H
.

G

Its negation
{G^{\bot}}
is shown on the right above.

{obs}

The dual graph construction defines the standard De
Morgan dualities relating conjunction and disjunction, i.e., for every
formula
\phi
, we have

\llbracket{\phi^{\bot}}\rrbracket\simeq{\llbracket\phi\rrbracket^{\bot}}
. De Morgan
dualities extended to prime graphs as

{P\llparenthesis M_{1},\ldots,M_{n}\rrparenthesis^{\bot}}\simeq{P^{\bot}}\llparenthesis{M_{1}^{\bot}},\ldots,{M_{n}^{\bot}}\rrparenthesis
, where
{P^{\bot}}
is
the dual graph of
P
. Furthermore,
{P^{\bot}}
is prime if and
only if
P
is prime. Thus each pair of prime graphs
P
and

{P^{\bot}}
defines a pair of connectives that are De Morgan duals to
each other.

We will now develop our proof system based on the above notion of
negation as graph duality. The requirements mentioned in the
introduction entail that:

(1)

for any isomorphic graphs
G
and
H
, the graph

G\multimap H
should be provable;

(2)

if
G\neq\varnothing
then

G
and
{G^{\bot}}
should not be both provable;

(3)

the implication
\multimap
should be transitive, i.e., if
G\multimap H
, and

H\multimap K
are provable then so should be
G\multimap K
;

(4)

the implication
\multimap
should be closed under context,
i.e., if
G\multimap H
is provable and

C[\cdot]_{R}
is an arbitrary context, then

C[G]_{R}\multimap C[H]_{R}
should be provable;

(5)

if
A
and
C
are provable graphs, and
R\subseteq V_{C}
,
then the graph
C[A]_{R}
should also be provable.

As our chosen notation suggests, our proof system will be an extension of multiplicative linear logic (MLL). Note that this is not our starting point, but a consequence of the conditions above. Since we have a common unit for
\mathbin{\invamp}
and
\mathbin{\otimes}
, namely the empty graph, a form of
mix
(i.e.,
A\mathbin{\otimes}B\multimap A\mathbin{\invamp}B
) will be derivable in our system. Indeed, it turns out that our proof system is a conservative extension of MLL with mix
[
Gir87a
,
Bel97
,
FR94
]
. This will be discussed in detail in Section
8
.

This example also shows that that implication is not simply subset inclusion of
edges. However, in our minimal logic on graphs that we present here, the converse does hold: we will see later that whenever we
have that
G\multimap H

V_{G}=V_{H}
then
E_{H}\subseteq E_{G}
.

6

But this
observation is not true in general for all logics that might be designed on graphs. For example
in the extension of Boolean logic, defined in
[
CDW20
]
,
is is not necessarily true that implication preserves edges.

For presenting the inference system we use a
deep inference

formalism
[
GS01
,
Gug07
]
, which allows rewriting inside an
arbitrary context and admits a rather flexible composition of
derivations. In our presentation we will follow the notation of

open deduction
, introduced in
[
GGP10
]
.

Let us start with the following two inference rules

\varnothing

\scriptstyle\mathsf{i}\mathord{\downarrow}\;

{A^{\bot}}\mathbin{\invamp}A

B\mathbin{\otimes}A

\scriptstyle\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\uparrow}\;

\scriptstyle\;~~S\subseteq V_{B},~S\neq V_{B}

B[A]_{S}

(16)

which are induced by the two Points
1
and

above, and which are called

Definition 13
.

Definition 14

super switch up, respectively.
The
\mathsf{i}\mathord{\downarrow}
says that for arbitrary graphs
C
and
A
and any

R\subseteq V_{C}
, if
C
is provable, then so is the graph

C[A\mathbin{\invamp}{A^{\bot}}]_{R}
. Similarly, the rule
\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\uparrow}
says that
whenever
C[B\mathbin{\otimes}A]_{R}
is provable, then so is

C[B[A]_{S}]_{R}
for any three graphs
A
,
B
,
C

and any
R\subseteq V_{C}
and
S\subseteq V_{B}
. The condition
S\neq V_{B}

is there to avoid a trivial rule instance, as

B[A]_{S}=B\mathbin{\otimes}A
if
S=V_{B}
. Practically, the rule

\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\uparrow}
only removes some of the edges between the modules
A
and
B
in
the graph
C[B\mathbin{\otimes}A]_{R}
. But it is important to observe
that we cannot simply remove arbitrary edges. We always have to ensure
that
A
remains a module in the resulting graph. More precisely, in
B\mathbin{\otimes}A
, both
B
and
A
are modules, but in
B[A]_{S}
only
A
is a module, but
B
is not.

As the name “deep inference” suggests, we want to apply the inference rules inside any context
C[\cdot]_{R}
, and not only at the top level in the modular decomposition tree. For this, we define now how we build derivations from inference rules.

). This concerns also situations
as shown below left, which are written as shown below right:

{\fcolorbox{currentcolor!0}{currentcolor!5}{$\vcenter{\copy\derboxone}$}}\qquad\leadsto\qquad{\fcolorbox{currentcolor!0}{currentcolor!5}{$\vcenter{\copy\derboxone}$}}\quad\mbox{or}\quad{\fcolorbox{currentcolor!0}{currentcolor!5}{$\vcenter{\copy\derboxone}$}}

(20)

In other words, in derivations, we consider graphs equal modulo
isomorphisms. In particular, for the length
|\mathcal{D}|
of a
derivation, we count only the inference steps that are not
isomorphisms. This abuse of notation is justified as these
isomorphisms can be permuted with all inference rules that we
discuss in this paper. Furthermore, when we draw the graphs as in
(
21
) below, the isomorphisms are not visible.

{exa}

only
\mathsf{i}\mathord{\downarrow}
and
\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\uparrow}

Remark 22
.

In
[
GGP10
]
it is shown how a derivation on formulas
in the style of open deduction (as we defined it in
Definition
14
), can be translated into a derivation
in the style of the calculus of
structures
[
Gug07
,
GS01
]
, which can be seen as a
sequence of rewriting steps on formulas. The same also works on derivations for
graphs. To give an example, consider the derivation on the left
below:

\small{\fcolorbox{currentcolor!0}{currentcolor!5}{$\vcenter{\copy\derboxone}$}}\hskip 9.24994pt\leadsto\hskip 9.24994pt{\fcolorbox{currentcolor!0}{currentcolor!5}{$\vcenter{\copy\derboxone}$}}

(23)

which can also be written as shown on the right above. (Note that we
make use of the notation
in (
19
)). In
[
GGP10
]
, the
derivation on the left in (
23
) is called

Definition 23
.

synchronal
and the one on the right in (
23
) is called

Definition 24
.

sequential. For every synchronal
derivation there is at least one sequential variant (but it is
not unique). In later parts of the paper we sometimes speak of the “bottommost” rule
instance in a derivation. In these cases, we assume that we have fixed some sequential form.
Observe that both derivations in (
23
) above make
use of (
20
).

As in other deep inference systems, we can give for the rules in (
16
) their
duals
. In general, if

G

\scriptstyle\mathsf{r}\;

H

is an instance of a rule, then

{H^{\bot}}

\scriptstyle{\mathsf{r}^{\bot}}\;

{G^{\bot}}

is an instance of the dual rule. The duals of the two rules in (
16
) are the following:

A\mathbin{\otimes}{A^{\bot}}

\scriptstyle\mathsf{i}\mathord{\uparrow}\;

\varnothing

B[A]_{S}

\scriptstyle\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\downarrow}\;

\scriptstyle\;~~S\subseteq V_{B},~S\neq\varnothing

B\mathbin{\invamp}A

(24)

called

Definition 25
.

identity up (or

Definition 26
.

cut) and

Definition 27
.

super switch
down, respectively.
We have the side condition
S\neq\varnothing
to avoid a triviality, as

B[A]_{S}=B\mathbin{\invamp}A
if
S=\varnothing
. Dually to
\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\uparrow}
, the

\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\downarrow}
-rule removes all the edges between
A
and
B
.

{defi}

Let
\mathsf{S}
be an inference system. We say that an inference rule

\mathsf{r}
is

Definition 28
.

derivable in
\mathsf{S}
iff

\mbox{for every instance}\enskip{\vbox{\hbox{\kern 5.16939pt\hbox{\vbox{\hbox{\kern 0.63124pt\hbox{\hbox{\hbox{$G$}}}\kern 0.63124pt}\kern 1.43518pt\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\hbox{$\smash{\lower 2.5pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{r}\;$}}$}}\vbox{\vbox to0.4pt{\vfill\hbox to9.12497pt{\leaders{\hrule}{\hfill}\kern 0.0pt}\vfill}}\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{$\smash{\lower 2.5pt\hbox{$$}}$}\hss}}\kern 1.43518pt\hbox{\hbox{\hbox{$\kern 0.43752pt\hbox{$H$}\kern 0.43752pt$}}}}}\kern 0.0pt}}}\quad\mbox{there is a derivation}\enskip\smash{{{{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}}{{{}}}\fcolorbox{currentcolor!0}{currentcolor!5}{$\vcenter{\copy\derboxone}$}}}\;\;.

We say that
\mathsf{r}
is

Definition 29
.

admissible in
\mathsf{S}
iff

\mbox{for every instance}\enskip{\vbox{\hbox{\kern 5.16939pt\hbox{\vbox{\hbox{\kern 0.63124pt\hbox{\hbox{\hbox{$G$}}}\kern 0.63124pt}\kern 1.43518pt\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\hbox{$\smash{\lower 2.5pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mathsf{r}\;$}}$}}\vbox{\vbox to0.4pt{\vfill\hbox to9.12497pt{\leaders{\hrule}{\hfill}\kern 0.0pt}\vfill}}\hbox to0.0pt{\hbox{$\smash{\lower 2.5pt\hbox{$$}}$}\hss}}\kern 1.43518pt\hbox{\hbox{\hbox{$\kern 0.43752pt\hbox{$H$}\kern 0.43752pt$}}}}}\kern 0.0pt}}}\quad\mbox{we have that~~}\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{S}}\,}{G}\mbox{~~implies~~}\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{S}}\,}{H}\;\,.

If
\mathsf{r}\in\mathsf{S}
then
\mathsf{r}
is trivially derivable and admissible in
\mathsf{S}
.

,

.

switch rule:

.

(26)

One can immediately see that it is its own dual and is a special case of both

\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\downarrow}
and
\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\uparrow}
. We therefore have the following:

Lemma 4.1
.

If in an inference system
\mathsf{S}
one of the rules
\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\downarrow}
and

\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\uparrow}
is derivable, then so is
\mathsf{sw}
.

Remark 31
.

In a standard deep inference system for formulas we
also have the converse of Lemma
4.1
, i.e., if
\mathsf{sw}

is derivable, then so are
\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\uparrow}
and
\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\downarrow}
(see,
e.g.,
[
Str03a
]
). However, in the case of
arbitrary graphs this is no longer true, and the rules
\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\uparrow}
and

\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\downarrow}
are strictly more powerful than
\mathsf{sw}
.

Lemma 4.2
.

Let
\mathsf{S}
be an inference system. If the rules
\mathsf{i}\mathord{\downarrow}
and

\mathsf{i}\mathord{\uparrow}
and
\mathsf{sw}
are derivable in
\mathsf{S}
, then for every
rule
\mathsf{r}
that is derivable in
\mathsf{S}
, also its dual
{\mathsf{r}^{\bot}}
is
derivable in
\mathsf{S}
.

Proof 4.3
.

Suppose we have two graphs
G
and
H
, and a derivation from

G
to
H
in
\mathsf{S}
. Then it suffices to show that we can
construct a derivation from
{H^{\bot}}
to
{G^{\bot}}
in
\mathsf{S}
:

{\fcolorbox{currentcolor!0}{currentcolor!10}{$\vcenter{\copy\derboxone}$}}\mathbin{\otimes}{H^{\bot}}

\scriptstyle\mathsf{sw}\;

{G^{\bot}}\mathbin{\invamp}{\fcolorbox{currentcolor!0}{currentcolor!10}{$\vcenter{\copy\derboxone}$}}

Note that
\varnothing\mathbin{\otimes}{H^{\bot}}={H^{\bot}}
and
{G^{\bot}}\mathbin{\invamp}\varnothing={G^{\bot}}
.

Lemma 4.4
.

If the rules
\mathsf{i}\mathord{\uparrow}
and
\mathsf{sw}
are admissible for an inference
system
\mathsf{S}
, then
\multimap
is transitive, i.e., if

\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{S}}\,}{G\multimap H}
and
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{S}}\,}{H\multimap K}
then

\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{S}}\,}{G\multimap K}
.

Proof 4.5
.

We can construct the following derivation

{{{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}}{{{}}}\fcolorbox{currentcolor!0}{currentcolor!10}{$\vcenter{\copy\derboxone}$}}\mathbin{\otimes}{{{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}}{{{}}}\fcolorbox{currentcolor!0}{currentcolor!10}{$\vcenter{\copy\derboxone}$}}

\scriptstyle\mathsf{sw}\;

{G^{\bot}}\mathbin{\invamp}{\fcolorbox{currentcolor!0}{currentcolor!10}{$\vcenter{\copy\derboxone}$}}

(27)

from
\varnothing
to
{G^{\bot}}\mathbin{\invamp}K
in
\mathsf{S}
.

Lemma
4.4
is the reason why
\mathsf{i}\mathord{\uparrow}
is also called
cut
.
In a well-designed deep inference system for formulas, the two rules

\mathsf{i}\mathord{\downarrow}
and
\mathsf{i}\mathord{\uparrow}
can be restricted in a way that they are only
applicable to atoms, i.e., replaced by the following two rules that we
call

Definition 32
.

atomic identity down and

Definition 33
.

atomic identity up,
respectively:

\varnothing

\scriptstyle\mathsf{ai}\mathord{\downarrow}\;

{a^{\bot}}\mathbin{\invamp}a

and

a\mathbin{\otimes}{a^{\bot}}

\scriptstyle\mathsf{ai}\mathord{\uparrow}\;

\varnothing

(28)

We would like to achieve something similar for our proof system on
graphs. For this it is necessary to be able to decompose prime graphs
into atoms, but the two rules
\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\downarrow}
and
\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\uparrow}
cannot do this, as
they are only able to move around modules in a graph. For this reason,
we add the following two rules to our system:

{({M_{1}\mathbin{\mathbin{\invamp}}N_{1}})\mathbin{\varotimes}\cdots\mathbin{\varotimes}({M_{n}\mathbin{\mathbin{\invamp}}N_{n}})}

\scriptstyle\mathsf{p}\mathord{\downarrow}\;

\scriptstyle\;~P\text{~prime,~}|V_{P}|\geq 4,~M_{1}\neq\varnothing,\ldots,M_{n}\neq\varnothing

P\llparenthesis M_{1},\ldots,M_{n}\rrparenthesis\mathbin{\invamp}{P^{\bot}}\llparenthesis N_{1},\ldots,N_{n}\rrparenthesis

(29)

called

Definition 34
.

prime down, and

P\llparenthesis M_{1},\ldots,M_{n}\rrparenthesis\mathbin{\otimes}{P^{\bot}}\llparenthesis N_{1},\ldots,N_{n}\rrparenthesis

\scriptstyle\mathsf{p}\mathord{\uparrow}\;

\scriptstyle\;~P\text{~prime,~}|V_{P}|\geq 4~M_{1}\neq\varnothing,\ldots,M_{n}\neq\varnothing

{({M_{1}\mathbin{\varotimes}N_{1}})\mathbin{\mathbin{\invamp}}\cdots\mathbin{\mathbin{\invamp}}({M_{n}\mathbin{\varotimes}N_{n}})}

(30)

called

Definition 35
.

prime up. In both cases, the side condition is that

P
needs to be a prime graph and has at least
4

vertices.
We also require that for all
i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}
we have that
M_{i}
is non-empty
in an application of
\mathsf{p}\mathord{\downarrow}
and
\mathsf{p}\mathord{\uparrow}
.
8
8

8

In the conference version
[
AHS20
]
of this paper,
we had the weaker condition that for all
i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}
at
least one of
M_{i}
and
N_{i}
is non-empty. The advantage of the
stronger condition that we use here is that we obtain a more
controlled proof system as the prime graphs involved in
a
\mathsf{p}\mathord{\downarrow}
can only be those that appear in the modular decomposition
of the graph.

The reason for the side conditions on the
\mathsf{p}\mathord{\downarrow}
is
not that the rules would become unsound otherwise. In fact, these
rules without side conditions are admissible in the general case. The
details will be discussed in the proof of Lemma
5.1
and at the end of Section
7
.

5.
Properties of the Proof System

The properties that we establish here are standard for deep inference systems (see, e.g.,
[
GS01
,
TS19
]
).
The first observation about
\mathsf{SGS}
is that the general forms of the
identity rules
\mathsf{i}\mathord{\downarrow}
and
\mathsf{i}\mathord{\uparrow}
are derivable, as we will see in
Corollary

below. Before, we show an auxiliary lemma stating the corresponding result for the
prime rules, namely that their general form is also derivable, i.e., they
can be applied to any graph instead of only prime graphs.

Lemma 5.1
.

Let

G\llparenthesis M_{1},\ldots,M_{n}\rrparenthesis\mathbin{\invamp}{G^{\bot}}\llparenthesis N_{1},\ldots,N_{n}\rrparenthesis

G\llparenthesis M_{1},\ldots,M_{n}\rrparenthesis\mathbin{\otimes}{G^{\bot}}\llparenthesis N_{1},\ldots,N_{n}\rrparenthesis

.

{obs}

The system
\mathsf{GS}
forms a proof system in the sense of Cook and
Reckhow
[
CR79
]
, as the time complexity of checking the
correct application of each inference step is polynomial. Note that the modular
decomposition of graphs can be obtained in linear
time
[
MS94
]
. Furthermore, the use of the graph isomorphisms
for the composition of derivations, as in (
17
), does not
increase complexity, as we assume that the isomorphism
f
is
explicitly given, such that the correctness of the operation can
also be checked in linear time.

Let us now define the notion of
size

of a graph that will play a central role in the normalisation proof as
an induction measure.

{defi}

The
size
of a graph
G
, denoted by
|\mkern-2.75mu|G|\mkern-2.75mu|
, is the
lexicographic pair
\langle|V_{G}|,|E_{{G^{\bot}}}|\rangle
. That is, if

G
and
H
are graphs, then
|\mkern-2.75mu|G|\mkern-2.75mu|<|\mkern-2.75mu|H|\mkern-2.75mu|
if

|V_{G}|<|V_{H}|
or if
|V_{G}|=|V_{H}|
and

|E_{{G^{\bot}}}|<|E_{{H^{\bot}}}|
.

{obs}

Every
inference rule discussed so far, except for
\mathsf{ai}\mathord{\uparrow}
and
\mathsf{i}\mathord{\uparrow}
do
strictly decrease the size of a graph when going bottom-up in a
derivation. That is, whenever we have an instance

H

\scriptstyle\mathsf{r}\;

G

of an inference rule

\mathsf{r}\in\{\mathsf{ai}\mathord{\downarrow},\mathsf{i}\mathord{\downarrow},\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\downarrow},\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\uparrow},\mathsf{p}\mathord{\downarrow},\mathsf{p}\mathord{\uparrow},\mathsf{g}\mathord{\downarrow},\mathsf{g}\mathord{\uparrow}\}
, then

|\mkern-2.75mu|H|\mkern-2.75mu|<|\mkern-2.75mu|G|\mkern-2.75mu|
.
Since each such inference step either reduces the number of vertices or the number of edges in the dual graph (or both), and these numbers are never increased, the length of a derivation in

\mathsf{GS}
with conclusion
G
is bound by
n^{2}+n
where
n=|V_{G}|
is
the number of vertices in
G
.
9
9

9

For the case that the derivation contains only cographs, it can in fact be shown that the length
is bound by
\frac{1}{2}n^{2}
(see
[
BS17
]
), but as the details
are not needed for this paper, we leave them to the reader.

Furthermore, to each graph only finitely many different non-trivial inference steps can be applied, and every derivation can be reorganised such that between any two (non-trivial) inference steps (see Remark
22
) there is at most one isomorphism step.
Hence, it follows immediately that provability in
\mathsf{GS}
is decidable and in

NP
. In Section
8
we are going to show that it is also
NP
-hard, and therefore
NP
-complete.

6.
Splitting and Context Reduction

We are now ready to present the fundamental properties of the system

\mathsf{GS}
, namely the
splitting lemmas
and
context
reduction
, that allow to prove cut elimination in the next section.
10
10

10

Proceeding via splitting and context reduction is not the only method to prove cut elimination for a deep inference proof system (see e.g.
[
Brü03
,
Str03b
,
AG21
]
), but it is the most organized and most universal method, and at the current state of art, it seems to be the only one that is applicable to
\mathsf{GS}
.

First, recall that the standard syntactic method for proving cut elimination in the
sequent calculus is to permute the cut rule upwards in the proof,
while decomposing the cut formula along its main connective, and so
inductively reduce the cut rank. However, in systems formulated using
deep inference this method cannot be applied, as derivations can be
constructed in a more flexible way than in the sequent calculus. For
this reason, the
splitting
technique has been developed in the
literature on deep
inference
[
Gug07
,
Str03a
,
GS11
,
HTAC19
,
AT17
]
. In
this section we discuss how to prove the splitting and the context
reduction lemmas for our system and how their proofs differs form the
ones in the literature. The detailed proofs of the statement in this
section can be found in Appendix
A
.

From sequent calculus to splitting for graphs.

Consider the typical rule for
\mathbin{\otimes}
in the sequent calculus.

\Gamma,\phi\;\;

\;\;\Delta,\psi

\scriptstyle\mathbin{\otimes}\;

\Gamma,\phi\mathbin{\otimes}\psi,\Delta

The effect of the above rule can be simulated by applying the following splitting lemma for the prime graph
\mathbin{\otimes}
.

Lemma 6.1

(Splitting Tensor)
.

Let
G
,
A
and
B
be graphs.
If
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{GS}}\,}{G\mathbin{\invamp}(A\mathbin{\otimes}B)}
then there is a context
C
and there are graphs
K_{A}
and
K_{B}

such that
there are derivations

{{{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}}{{{}}}\fcolorbox{currentcolor!0}{currentcolor!5}{$\vcenter{\copy\derboxone}$}}\;,\;{{{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}}{{{}}}\fcolorbox{currentcolor!0}{currentcolor!5}{$\vcenter{\copy\derboxone}$}}\;,\;{{{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}}{{{}}}\fcolorbox{currentcolor!0}{currentcolor!5}{$\vcenter{\copy\derboxone}$}}\quad\mbox{and}\quad{{{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}}{{{}}}\fcolorbox{currentcolor!0}{currentcolor!5}{$\vcenter{\copy\derboxone}$}}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip 10.22217pt.\hss}

The graphs
A
and
B
in Lemma
6.1

play the role of formulas
\phi
and
\psi
in the sequent calculus rule
\mathbin{\otimes}
;
while
K_{A}
and
K_{B}
play the role of sequents
\Gamma
and
\Delta
.
Thus, when we say in Lemma
6.1
that
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{GS}}\,}{K_{A}\mathbin{\invamp}A}
and
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{GS}}\,}{K_{B}\mathbin{\invamp}B}
hold, this corresponds to the provability of the premises
\Gamma,\phi
and
\Delta,\psi
in the sequent calculus
\mathbin{\otimes}
-rule.
This means that Lemma
6.1
allows us to rewrite a sequent-like graph
G\mathbin{\invamp}(A\mathbin{\otimes}B)
into a form where the effect of the
\mathbin{\otimes}
-rule of the sequent calculus can be simulated.

Remark 50
.

Note that this splitting is fundamentally different from the
well-known
splitting tensor lemma
for MLL proof
nets
[
Gir87a
,
DR89
,
Ret96
]
. Whereas the
MLL splitting tensor lemma says that
there exists
at least
one tensor that is splitting, our splitting tensor lemma says that

every
tensor is splitting.

11

In the language of proof nets, our
splitting lemma says that every tensor is splitting for its empire

and
the proof system is expressive enough to reduce
everything else without touching that empire. However, for our graphs, we do not (yet) have a notion of
empire
.

Let us use the derivation in (
25
), recalled below in (
34
) for convenience, as an example to illustrate
this pattern.
Observe that the conclusion is of the form
G\mathbin{\invamp}(({a^{\bot}}\mathbin{\invamp}{c^{\bot}})\mathbin{\otimes}{b^{\bot}})
for some graph
G
,
and that after applying
\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\downarrow}
and
\mathsf{ai}\mathord{\downarrow}
we have split the graph
G
into two graph
K_{A}=a\mathbin{\otimes}c
and
K_{B}=b
,
such that
K_{A}\mathbin{\invamp}{a^{\bot}}\mathbin{\invamp}{c^{\bot}}
and
K_{B}\mathbin{\invamp}{b^{\bot}}
are provable.

(35)

which is of the form
G\mathbin{\invamp}(a\mathbin{\otimes}b)
for some
G

and
it is provable in
\mathsf{GS}
.
It is impossible however to apply a derivation to
G
to obtain two disjoint graphs
K_{A}
and
K_{B}
, such that
K_{A}\mathbin{\invamp}a
and
K_{B}\mathbin{\invamp}b
are provable, unless we define a suitable context for
K_{A}\mathbin{\invamp}K_{B}
.
Indeed we do have the following context formed from the provable graph
C={g^{\bot}}\mathbin{\invamp}{f^{\bot}}\mathbin{\invamp}(g\mathbin{\otimes}f)
.

C[\cdot]_{\{{f^{\bot}},f,g\}}=\begin{array}[]{c@{\quad\;\;}c@{\quad\;\;}c@{\quad\;\;}c@{\quad\;\;}c@{\quad\;\;}c@{\quad\;\;}c@{\quad\;\;}c@{\quad\;\;}c@{\quad\;\;}c}\mathord{\hbox to5.13pt{\vbox to10.43pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\>\lower-5.21722pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{
{}{}}}{

Following the naming convention in the statement of Lemma
6.1
,
we have
K_{A}={a^{\bot}}
and
K_{A}={b^{\bot}}
such that
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{GS}}\,}{K_{A}\mathbin{\invamp}a}
and
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{GS}}\,}{K_{B}\mathbin{\invamp}b}
hold, and furthermore
G
is formed from plugging
K_{A}\mathbin{\invamp}K_{B}
insider the above mentioned context formed from
C
.

From the above ingredients satisfying the condition of the splitting lemma we can always construct a proof.
We can apply
\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\downarrow}
twice to bring
K_{A}
and
a
together inside a context formed from
C
, and similarly for
K_{B}
and
b
.
After having completed the proofs that consume
a
and
b
(by a simple application of
\mathsf{ai}\mathord{\downarrow}
) we are left with the provable graph
C
.
The important observation here is that it is impossible to apply a derivation that changes the shape of
C
until we have completed the derivation that consumes
{a^{\bot}}
and
{b^{\bot}}
.

The problem illustrated above with the context
C
, that cannot be removed until the end of the proof, is a fundamental problem that we have with graphs and that we do not have with formulas. Essentially it is due to the presence of
\mathsf{P_{4}}
induced sub-graphs that create indirect dependencies between atoms, such as the indirect dependency between
{g^{\bot}}
and
g
in the above example.

Generalising splitting to prime graphs.

The general idea of
a splitting lemma is that, in a provable “sequent-like graph”, consisting of
a number of disjoint connected components, we can select any of these
components as the
principal graph
and apply a derivation to
the other components, such that eventually a rule breaking down the
principal component can be applied. This allows us to approximate the
effect of applying rules in the sequent calculus, even when no sequent calculus exists, as is the case when the principal graph is formed using a prime graph that is not a tensor.

Lemma 6.2

(Splitting Prime)
.

Let
G
be a graph
and

P\neq\mathbin{\invamp}
be a prime graph with
|V_{P}|=n
, and
M_{1},\dots,M_{n}
be non-empty graphs.
If
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{GS}}\,}{G\mathbin{\invamp}P\llparenthesis M_{1},\dots,M_{n}\rrparenthesis}
, then one of the following holds:

(1)

either there is a context
C[\cdot]_{R}

and graphs
K_{1}
, …,
K_{n}
,
such that
there are derivations

{{{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}}{{{}}}\fcolorbox{currentcolor!0}{currentcolor!5}{$\vcenter{\copy\derboxone}$}}\;,\;{{{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}}{{{}}}\fcolorbox{currentcolor!0}{currentcolor!5}{$\vcenter{\copy\derboxone}$}}\quad\mbox{and}\quad{{{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}}{{{}}}\fcolorbox{currentcolor!0}{currentcolor!5}{$\vcenter{\copy\derboxone}$}}

for all
i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}
,

(2)

or there is a context
C[\cdot]_{R}
and graphs
K_{X}
and
K_{Y}
,
such that
there are derivations

{{{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}}{{{}}}\fcolorbox{currentcolor!0}{currentcolor!5}{$\vcenter{\copy\derboxone}$}}\;,\;{{{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}}{{{}}}\fcolorbox{currentcolor!0}{currentcolor!5}{$\vcenter{\copy\derboxone}$}}\;,\;{{{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}}{{{}}}\fcolorbox{currentcolor!0}{currentcolor!5}{$\vcenter{\copy\derboxone}$}}\quad\mbox{and}\quad{{{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}}{{{}}}\fcolorbox{currentcolor!0}{currentcolor!5}{$\vcenter{\copy\derboxone}$}}

for some
i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}
.

Remark 51
.

The immediate question to address at this point is why we need two cases, where splitting lemmas in the literature require only one case.
Notice that Lemma
6.1
is a special case of Lemma
6.2
, since
\mathbin{\otimes}
is a prime graph, as indicated
in (
9
) in Section
3
.
In the case of the tensor, the two sub-cases of Lemma
6.2
collapse;
hence for
\mathbin{\otimes}
the above lemma for prime graphs collapses to the form of Lemma
6.1
.

The existence of these two separate cases is a surprising novelty
since all proof systems, on which the splitting technique has been applied so far,
only employ atoms, binary connectives
[
Gug07
,
AT17
]
, modalities
[
Str03a
,
GS11
]
, and quantifiers
[
HTAC19
]
. Here, for the first time we present splitting for
n
-ary connectives with
n>2
.

When the principal graph is formed using a prime graph with at least four vertices, the two cases of Lemma
6.1
are properly distinct.
We illustrate first the case
1
of Lemma
6.1
,
by renormalising the proof (
34
) as an example to explain
this idea.

In the conclusion of (
34
) we have the disjoint union of three connected
graphs.
We can select

\mathsf{P}_{4}\llparenthesis c,a,d,b\rrparenthesis
(the connected component on the right)
as
the principal component, and apply Case
1
of
Lemma
6.2
to
reorganise the derivation in such a way
an instance of
\mathsf{p}\mathord{\downarrow}

involving

\mathsf{P}_{4}\llparenthesis c,a,d,b\rrparenthesis

can be applied (see Example
35
).
This allows us to conclude as in Case
1
applies, since all of four graphs
{a^{\bot}}\mathbin{\invamp}a
,
{b^{\bot}}\mathbin{\invamp}b
,
{c^{\bot}}\mathbin{\invamp}c
and
{d^{\bot}}\mathbin{\invamp}d
are provable.
That is, we can obtain a derivation of the form

\varnothing

(37)

Here Case
1
cannot be applied since when we select

\mathsf{P}_{4}\llparenthesis c,{a^{\bot}},{b^{\bot}},{c^{\bot}}\rrparenthesis

as the principal component and we try to apply

\mathsf{p}\mathord{\downarrow}
, then
c
and
{c^{\bot}}
can no longer communicate.
Therefore, we must first move
a
or
b
into the structure and
apply an
\mathsf{ai}\mathord{\downarrow}
, in order to destroy the prime graph in such a way that
c
and
{c^{\bot}}
can still communicate.

to the graph
37

6.2
,

K_{X}=a
and
K_{Y}=b

Splitting for Atoms

We also need a splitting lemma where the principal graph is just a singleton.

Lemma 6.3

(Atomic Splitting)
.

Let
G
be a graph.
If
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{GS}}\,}{G\mathbin{\invamp}a}
for an atom
a
, then there is a context
C[\cdot]_{R}
such that
there are derivations

C[{a^{\bot}}]_{R}

\scriptstyle\scriptstyle\mathcal{D}_{G}\;

\scriptstyle\scriptstyle\;\mathsf{GS}

G

and

\varnothing

\scriptstyle\scriptstyle\mathcal{D}_{C}\;

\scriptstyle\scriptstyle\;\mathsf{GS}

C

.

Atomic splitting simply states that for an atom
a
in the proof, there is a matching
{a^{\bot}}
somewhere else in the proof. Note that there may be more than one
{a^{\bot}}
, in which case the lemma will pick out exactly the instance that interacts with
a
via an
\mathsf{ai}\mathord{\downarrow}
instance in the original proof.

As with splitting for prime graphs the novelty compared to the literature is the presence of the context
C
.

Context reduction.

Observe that the splitting lemma is not applied to a
\mathbin{\invamp}
-graph. The
\mathbin{\invamp}
plays in
\mathsf{GS}
a similar role as the comma in the sequent calculus.
Splitting lemmas such as Lemma
6.2
apply in a sequent-like
context, sometimes called a shallow context. Splitting cannot be applied to proofs where the principal graph (that is not a
\mathbin{\invamp}
) appears at any depth in the conclusion of the proof. In order to be able to use splitting to eliminate cuts at arbitrary depth, we need to extend splitting from shallow contexts to deep contexts. For this, we need the context reduction lemma, stated below.

Lemma 6.4

(Context reduction)
.

Let
A
be a graph and
G[\cdot]_{S}
be a context, such that

\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{GS}}\,}{G[A]_{S}}
. Then there are a
context
C[\cdot]_{R}
and a graph
K
, such that there are derivations

C[K\mathbin{\invamp}{\mathcal{X}}]_{R}

\scriptstyle\scriptstyle\mathcal{D}_{G}\;

\scriptstyle\scriptstyle\;\mathsf{GS}

G[{\mathcal{X}}]_{S}

and

\varnothing

\scriptstyle\scriptstyle\mathcal{D}_{A}\;

\scriptstyle\scriptstyle\;\mathsf{GS}

K\mathbin{\invamp}A

and

\varnothing

\scriptstyle\scriptstyle\mathcal{D}_{C}\;

\scriptstyle\scriptstyle\;\mathsf{GS}

C

for any graph
{\mathcal{X}}
.

The idea of context reduction is that, if we select any module, called
A
in Lemma
6.4
above, we can always rewrite its context, say
G[\cdot]_{S}
, such that it is of the form
K\mathbin{\invamp}[\cdot]_{\varnothing}
inside some provable context. The use of
{\mathcal{X}}
reflects the fact that, in doing so, you never need to change
A
; hence
A
could be replaced by another graph
{\mathcal{X}}
and the same transformation can be applied to the context.

Similarly to splitting, the novelty compared to context reduction in the literature is that we must keep track of a provable context.
This is required to cope with graphs such as the following:

{a^{\bot}}
in the above graph, and we wish to apply context reduction to it.
When we apply Lemma
6.4
, clearly there is only one choice of graph
K
such that
K\mathbin{\invamp}{a^{\bot}}
is provable, namely
K=a
.
Observe, furthermore, that in order to rewrite the rest of the above graph, so it is of the form
C[K\mathbin{\invamp}{a^{\bot}}]_{R}

such that
C
is provable, the only choice is to set
C={b^{\bot}}\mathbin{\invamp}{c^{\bot}}\mathbin{\invamp}(b\mathbin{\otimes}c)

Examples such as (
35
), (
37
) and (
40
), where each conclusion can only be proven if rules can be applied deep inside a graph instead of to a graph at the top level of the modular decomposition of the conclusion, show that deep inference is necessary for developing a proof theory on graphs allowing
\mathsf{P_{4}}
as an induced sub-graph.

Figure 2
.
A proof used to illustrate context reduction and splitting. It also shows a non-trivial use of the
\mathsf{p}\mathord{\downarrow}
-rule that cannot be achieved using the
\mathsf{i}\mathord{\downarrow}
-rule.

For a more substantial example consider the derivation in Figure
2
.
Assume, we aim to apply splitting to the
N
-shaped induced subgraph in the conclusion consisting of vertices labelled
c
,
{a^{\bot}}
,
{b^{\bot}}
and
{c^{\bot}}
.
Clearly, the splitting lemma cannot be directly applied to that induced subgraph,
so firstly we reduce the context.
The three bottommost inference steps shown in Figure
2
correspond to the steps taken by context reduction that do not touch the
N
-shaped subgraph but bring the vertices labelled
a
and
b
next to our subgraph.
At that point Case
2
of splitting for prime graphs can be applied to our
N
-shaped subgraph, taking into account that, together with the vertices labelled
a
and
b
, they form a sequent-like module of the graph at that point in the derivation. At this point, the splitting lemma provides us with the information needed to complete the proof.

An additional reason why Figure
2
is interesting is that it is an example of a proof where the effect of the
\mathsf{p}\mathord{\downarrow}
-rule cannot be simulated by using the
\mathsf{i}\mathord{\downarrow}
-rule.
Therefore, this example emphasises the need for
\mathsf{p}\mathord{\downarrow}
or at least a rule to the effect of
\mathsf{p}\mathord{\downarrow}
in an analytic proof system on graphs.

Proving splitting and context reduction.

The detailed proofs of these lemmas can be found in Appendix
A
. Here we present an outline and the basic ideas.
As standard, we proceed by exhausting all possible permutations of rules where the main points of interest are where the rules change the principal connective in some way.
The novelty compared to results in the literature on deep inference is that, due to the important role of contexts we prove splitting and context reduction together by mutual induction, using the size
|\mkern-2.75mu|G|\mkern-2.75mu|
of a graph (see Definition
5
) as induction measure.

During the proof of splitting and context reduction we must handle cases involving the
\mathsf{p}\mathord{\downarrow}
rule.
Observe that when the
\mathsf{p}\mathord{\downarrow}
rule is applied we obtain at least four graphs connected by tensors.
Since we will need to handle frequently such cases, we find it convenient to state splitting for such multi-tensors as a lemma.
In what follows we generalise the Lemma
6.1
to the
n
-ary tensor for any
n\geq 2
(or
multi-tensor
), which is clearly a consequence of splitting for tensor (which, in turn, we have discussed is a special case of splitting for prime graphs).

Lemma 6.5

(Splitting Multi-tensor)
.

Let
G
be a graph, and
A_{1},\dots,A_{n}
be non-empty graphs.
If
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{GS}}\,}{G\mathbin{\invamp}({A_{1}\mathbin{\otimes}\cdots\mathbin{\otimes}A_{n}})}
,
then there is a context
C[\cdot]_{R}
and graphs
K_{1}
, …,
K_{n}
,
such that
there are derivations

{{{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}}{{{}}}\fcolorbox{currentcolor!0}{currentcolor!5}{$\vcenter{\copy\derboxone}$}}\;,\;{{{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}}{{{}}}\fcolorbox{currentcolor!0}{currentcolor!5}{$\vcenter{\copy\derboxone}$}}\quad\mbox{and}\quad{{{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}{}}{{{}}}\fcolorbox{currentcolor!0}{currentcolor!5}{$\vcenter{\copy\derboxone}$}}\hskip-10.00002pt

for all
i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}
.

All lemmas of this section are proved simultaneously, by case analysis
and an inductive argument. Before we go into the details of the
case analysis, let us draw the attention to
Figure
3
, which shows in more detail the
dependencies of the proofs of all lemmas in this section.
The main lemma is Lemma
6.2
. Then
Lemma
6.1
is just a special case of
Lemma
6.2
, and
Lemma
6.5
follows immediately by iterating
Lemma
6.1
.
To ensure
that there is no circular reasoning in the other dependencies, we argue that whenever the proof
of one lemma refers to another then this happens with respect to a
strictly smaller graph (according to Definition
5
).
Let us now look more closely at the case analysis for Lemma
6.2
.

Case Analysis for the proof of Lemma
6.2
(Splitting Prime)

There are five cases to consider which we enumerate below.

(1)

The last rule in the given proof acts inside
G
or any
M_{i}
with
i\in\{1,\dots,n\}
.
This case is relatively simple, since the structure of the conclusion does not change.

(2)

The last rule in the given proof is a
\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\downarrow}
such that another graph, external to the principal prime graph, moves inside the principal prime graph, i.e.,

G=G^{\prime}\mathbin{\invamp}G^{\prime\prime}
with
G^{\prime}\neq\varnothing
and
\mathcal{D}
is of shape

\varnothing

\scriptstyle\scriptstyle\mathcal{D}^{\prime\prime}\;

\scriptstyle\scriptstyle\;\mathsf{GS}

G^{\prime\prime}\mathbin{\invamp}P\llparenthesis M_{1},\ldots,M_{n}\rrparenthesis[G^{\prime}]_{R_{P}}

\scriptstyle\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\downarrow}\;

G^{\prime\prime}\mathbin{\invamp}G^{\prime}\mathbin{\invamp}P\llparenthesis M_{1},\ldots,M_{n}\rrparenthesis

This can result in several scenarios, that are named
(b.I), (b.II), and (b.III) in the appendix, and that
are not all immediately obvious.

(3)

The last rule in the given proof is a
\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\downarrow}
that moves the whole prime graph inside the rest of the graph.
In this case

\mathcal{D}
is of shape

\varnothing

\scriptstyle\scriptstyle\mathcal{D}^{\prime}\;

\scriptstyle\scriptstyle\;\mathsf{GS}

G[P\llparenthesis M_{1},\ldots,M_{n}\rrparenthesis]_{S}

\scriptstyle\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\downarrow}\;

G\mathbin{\invamp}P\llparenthesis M_{1},\ldots,M_{n}\rrparenthesis

We will explain that this case appeals to context reduction.

(4)

The last rule in the given proof is a
\mathsf{p}\mathord{\downarrow}
directly applied to the principal connective,
i.e.,
G=G^{\prime}\mathbin{\invamp}{P^{\bot}}\llparenthesis N_{1},\ldots,N_{n}\rrparenthesis

and

\mathcal{D}
is of shape

{\fcolorbox{currentcolor!0}{currentcolor!5}{$\vcenter{\copy\derboxone}$}}\;.\hskip-30.00005pt

In this case we have to refer to the multi-tensor splitting lemma.

(5)

The last rule is a
\mathsf{p}\mathord{\downarrow}
such that not all components of the principal connective are non-empty, and we have

G=G^{\prime\prime}\mathbin{\invamp}Q\llparenthesis N_{1},\ldots,N_{k}\rrparenthesis
where
N_{1},\dots,N_{k}
are non-empty graphs,

Q
is a prime graph with
|V_{Q}|>|V_{P}|

and such that
w.l.o.g.

P\llparenthesis M_{1},\ldots,M_{n}\rrparenthesis={Q^{\bot}}\llparenthesis\varnothing,L_{2},\ldots L_{k}\rrparenthesis
for some (possibly empty) graphs
L_{2},\ldots L_{k}
,
and

\mathcal{D}
is of shape

\varnothing

\scriptstyle\scriptstyle\mathcal{D}^{\prime}\;

\scriptstyle\scriptstyle\;\mathsf{GS}

{G^{\prime\prime}\mathbin{\mathbin{\invamp}}({N_{1}\mathbin{\varotimes}({N_{2}\mathbin{\mathbin{\invamp}}L_{2}})\mathbin{\varotimes}\ldots\mathbin{\varotimes}({N_{k}\mathbin{\mathbin{\invamp}}L_{k}})})}

\scriptstyle\mathsf{p}\mathord{\downarrow}\;

{G^{\prime\prime}\mathbin{\mathbin{\invamp}}Q\llparenthesis N_{1},\ldots,N_{k}\rrparenthesis\mathbin{\mathbin{\invamp}}P\llparenthesis M_{1},\ldots,M_{n}\rrparenthesis}

In this case it is important to ensure the side-conditions on
\mathsf{p}\mathord{\downarrow}
are respected.

All technical details of this case analysis are in Appendix
A
. In the remainder of this section, we give some informal explanation why the cases in the proof of Lemma
6.2
can become complex. For this, consider the following example.

(41)

One possible way to prove the above graph is to first apply the
\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\downarrow}
-rule to move the vertex labelled
e
so that it is attached by an edge only to
h
. This way we obtain exactly the graph in the conclusion of Figure
2
, therefore we know already how to complete the proof via that strategy.

Now observe that the above graph (
41
) is of the form
G\mathbin{\invamp}((a\mathbin{\invamp}b)\mathbin{\otimes}(h\mathbin{\invamp}d))
. Thus it is in a form to which we could apply tensor splitting (Lemma
6.1
) to this
\mathbin{\otimes}
-operator as the principal graph. This forces the proof to be renormalised such that firstly
e
moves next to
{e^{\bot}}
as shown in the derivation below.

Observe that in the topmost graph in the derivation above we have broken the graph on the left into two disjoint graphs. The first is provable when composed with
a\mathbin{\invamp}b
, while the second is provable when composed with
d\mathbin{\invamp}h
.

The choices between the different rules to first apply to graph (
41
), where
\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\downarrow}
is applied to
e
in order to either create a larger prime graph on the right (leading to the proof in Figure
2
) or to break up the structure on the left as shown above, lead to quite different proofs. Moving from the former to the latter proof is discussed in Case
2c
in the proof of Lemma
6.2
, which is in fact the most involved sub-case.

Case
2b
in the proof of Lemma
6.2
is not immediately obvious but is nonetheless usually present in standard splitting proofs on formulas, where similar cases are induced by associativity. A typical example is given by the following two isomorphic graphs, that are composed differently:

2b
in the proof of Lemma

(43)

Case
2c
is then used to renormalise the proof of (
43
) such that the
P_{5}
on the left is split into two parts, from which we can reassemble a proof of the graph in the conclusion of (
42
) which satisfies the conditions of splitting for the tensor that we selected.
In particular, if
A=e\mathbin{\otimes}(a\mathbin{\invamp}b)
and
B=c\mathbin{\invamp}d
in Lemma
6.1
, then we obtain
K_{A}=({a^{\bot}}\mathbin{\otimes}{b^{\bot}})\mathbin{\invamp}{e^{\bot}}
and
K_{B}={c^{\bot}}\mathbin{\invamp}{d^{\bot}}
, as required (the context is empty for this example).

Beyond the above two illustrative examples of non-trivial normalisation steps, observe that the deepest nesting in the proof of splitting for prime graphs is inside Case
2c
, which has two more levels of nested case analysis to cover all ways in which we can handle situations where the principal graph is turned into a larger prime graph using the
\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\downarrow}
rule.

7.
Elimination of the Up-Fragment

We do now have all ingredients to prove the cut elimination result, i.e., the rule
\mathsf{i}\mathord{\uparrow}
is admissible for
\mathsf{GS}
(Theorem
42
). Recall that this is equivalent to the admissibility of the up-rules
\mathsf{ai}\mathord{\uparrow}
,
\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\uparrow}
, and
\mathsf{p}\mathord{\uparrow}
(Theorem
43
), and that this entails the transitivity of the consequence relation (Lemma
4.4
) and consistency of the proof system (Corollary
49
).

In this section we are going to show how splitting and context reduction
are employed to prove this result.
The procedure is similar to ordinary deep inference systems (see, e.g.,

[
Str03a
,
GS11
,
HTAC19
,
CGS11
]
).

\mathsf{ai}\mathord{\uparrow}

\mathsf{GS}
.

This proof is slightly different from the previous two and from what usually happens in a deep inference setting. In particular, we

lemma.

Alternative formulations of the rules of
\mathsf{GS}

Further admissibility results follow immediately without having to pass via splitting and context reduction, now that we have established cut elimination.
We can in fact considerably strengthen Theorem
43
, as follows.

Corollary 55
.

Let
\mathsf{r}
be an inference rule. If for every instance

A

\scriptstyle\mathsf{r}\;

B

of that rule we have
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{GS}}\,}{A\multimap B}
, then
\mathsf{r}
is admissible for
\mathsf{GS}
.

Proof 7.4
.

Assume we have
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{GS}}\,}{A}
. By
Corollary
45
we have a derivation in
\mathsf{SGS}
from

A
to
B
. Hence, we have
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{SGS}}\,}{B}
, and therefore by Corollary
44
also
\mathord{\vdash_{\mathsf{GS}}\,}{B}
.

Now consider the following two inference rules:

{({M_{1}\mathbin{\mathbin{\invamp}}N_{1}})\mathbin{\varotimes}\cdots\mathbin{\varotimes}({M_{n}\mathbin{\mathbin{\invamp}}N_{n}})}

\scriptstyle\mathsf{g}\mathord{\downarrow}\;

G\llparenthesis M_{1},\ldots,M_{n}\rrparenthesis\mathbin{\invamp}{G^{\bot}}\llparenthesis N_{1},\ldots,N_{n}\rrparenthesis

G\llparenthesis M_{1},\ldots,M_{n}\rrparenthesis\mathbin{\otimes}{G^{\bot}}\llparenthesis N_{1},\ldots,N_{n}\rrparenthesis

\scriptstyle\mathsf{g}\mathord{\uparrow}\;

{({M_{1}\mathbin{\varotimes}N_{1}})\mathbin{\mathbin{\invamp}}\cdots\mathbin{\mathbin{\invamp}}({M_{n}\mathbin{\varotimes}N_{n}})}

(44)

Their shape is similar to
\mathsf{p}\mathord{\downarrow}
and
\mathsf{p}\mathord{\uparrow}
, but there are no side
conditions, i.e.,
G
can be any graph, and there are no emptiness
or non-emptiness conditions for
M_{i}
or
N_{i}
.

Corollary 56
.

The two rules
\mathsf{g}\mathord{\downarrow}
and
\mathsf{g}\mathord{\uparrow}
are admissible for
\mathsf{GS}
.

Proof 7.5
.

We are going to show that for all graphs
G
with

and graphs

(45)

Then this corollary follows via Corollaries

and
55

), we use the following derivation

\varnothing

\scriptstyle n\times\mathsf{i}\mathord{\downarrow}\;

(({M_{1}^{\bot}}\mathbin{\otimes}{N_{1}^{\bot}})\mathbin{\invamp}M_{1}\mathbin{\invamp}N_{1})\mathbin{\otimes}\cdots\mathbin{\otimes}(({M_{n}^{\bot}}\mathbin{\otimes}{N_{n}^{\bot}})\mathbin{\invamp}M_{n}\mathbin{\invamp}N_{n})

\scriptstyle\scriptstyle\mathcal{D}\;

\scriptstyle\scriptstyle\;\mathsf{GS}

G\llparenthesis({M_{1}^{\bot}}\mathbin{\otimes}{N_{1}^{\bot}})\mathbin{\invamp}M_{1},\ldots,({M_{n}^{\bot}}\mathbin{\otimes}{N_{n}^{\bot}})\mathbin{\invamp}M_{n}\rrparenthesis\mathbin{\invamp}{G^{\bot}}\llparenthesis N_{1},\ldots,N_{n}\rrparenthesis

\scriptstyle n\times\mathsf{s\mkern-1.0mu.\mkern-1.0musw}\mathord{\downarrow}\;

({M_{1}^{\bot}}\mathbin{\otimes}{N_{1}^{\bot}})\mathbin{\invamp}\cdots\mathbin{\invamp}({M_{n}^{\bot}}\mathbin{\otimes}{N_{n}^{\bot}})\mathbin{\invamp}{G\llparenthesis M_{1},\ldots,M_{n}\rrparenthesis\mathbin{\invamp}{G^{\bot}}\llparenthesis N_{1},\ldots,N_{n}\rrparenthesis}

where
\mathcal{D}
exists by Lemma
5.1
. To see this, observe that
for each
i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}
, there are two cases: either

({M_{i}^{\bot}}\mathbin{\otimes}{N_{i}^{\bot}})\mathbin{\invamp}M_{i}\neq\varnothing
or

({M_{i}^{\bot}}\mathbin{\otimes}{N_{i}^{\bot}})\mathbin{\invamp}M_{i}=\varnothing
. In the second
case we also have
{N_{i}^{\bot}}=\varnothing
, and therefore also

N_{i}=\varnothing
. Hence, the condition for applying Lemma
5.1

is fulfilled.

The above corollary shows that a variant of
\mathsf{GS}
where we use
\mathsf{g}\mathord{\downarrow}
instead of
\mathsf{p}\mathord{\downarrow}
is equivalent to the system
\mathsf{GS}
using only
\mathsf{p}\mathord{\downarrow}
, as it is defined in Figure
1
.
Indeed, as noted previously in Section
4
, a weaker constraint on the
\mathsf{p}\mathord{\downarrow}
and
\mathsf{p}\mathord{\uparrow}
was used in the conference version of this paper
[
AHS20
]
,
which did not insist that all of the components of one graph are non-empty when applying these rules. Thus we have tightened the proof search space of
\mathsf{GS}
, but have not changed the expressive power of the logic.

The reason why it is not immediately obvious whether the stronger side conditions in this version of paper can be used, is that Corollary
56
is a proper admissibility result rather than a derivability result. As shown in Lemma
5.1
, if we drop the condition in
\mathsf{p}\mathord{\downarrow}
that
P
is prime then the rule for general graphs is derivable.
However, the condition that all components of one graph are non-empty is more subtle, since the resulting variant of
\mathsf{p}\mathord{\downarrow}
without that side-condition is not derivable using the rules of
\mathsf{GS}
with the side-conditions fixed in Figure
1
.
For a counterexample to the derivability of the unconstrained
\mathsf{g}\mathord{\downarrow}
rule in
\mathsf{GS}
, consider the proof on the left below and observe that the instance of
\mathsf{g}\mathord{\downarrow}
cannot be derived using the rules of
\mathsf{GS}
.
